On a four-node, 16-GPU cluster, DexAttention achieves a $1.39\times$ geometric-mean end-to-end training speedup over the fastest applicable baseline across 11 configurations. For dynamic video attention, it achieves $2.11$--$2.37\times$ speedups over Ring Attention including planning.

papers.title: Aggron: Aggressive Compression of Agentic KV Caches during Head-of-Line Stalls in the Request Queue
papers.abstract: LLM agents run long, multi-turn programs whose contexts grow at every step, and serving them is limited by KV cache capacity. To alleviate this limitation, systems use context compression techniques, which typically wait until the KV cache crosses a large threshold and then summarize large spans of history at once, either in the background while the agent progresses or on the critical path. These summarizations can be done using the same model running on the same engine, or using the same or a different model running on extra hardware. When running on the same engine, summarization competes with the requests being served for both compute and memory capacity. To maximize the cost-effectiveness of summarization, this paper presents a new serving system called {\em Aggron}. Aggron summarizes agentic requests at every turn and selectively summarizes only certain parts of the KV cache. As a result, Aggron retains accuracy and keeps summarization requests lightweight. Moreover, Aggron launches summarization requests from a separate {\em Summarization Queue} while the corresponding agentic request whose KV cache we want to compress is stalled in the main request queue due to head-of-line stalls. The Summarization queue utilizes compute and memory capacity left over by the head-of-line stalls in the main queue. Further, to maximize efficiency, the server issues summarizations only when it predicts that they can complete before the corresponding agentic request will finally execute. In our evaluation, we compare Aggron to state-of-the-art asynchronous summarization. At high load, Aggron reduces P99 program latency by $27$--$31\%$, and raises throughput by $1.34$--$1.40\times$.

papers.title: FOREST: Coordinating Tree-based HBF, RRAM, and HBM for Efficient Speculative LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by combining lightweight drafting with parallel target-model verification. However, its stages impose distinct resource demands: target verification requires high-throughput access to large weight sets, sequential drafting executes a compact model under tight latency constraints, and long-context attention processes growing key-value (KV) caches. Conventional GPU-centric SD systems serve these workloads through shared HBM-centric memory and general-purpose compute, creating mismatches in capacity, bandwidth, and computation. These mismatches constrain deployable model-context configurations and limit the efficiency of bandwidth-bound and latency-sensitive operations. We propose FOREST, a heterogeneous memory-centric architecture coordinating HBF, 3D-stacked RRAM, and HBM memory-compute trees for efficient SD. It features: (1) compute-aligned 3D RRAM, combining ultra-wide, low-frequency reads with clock-decoupled interfaces and overlapped SRAM-DCIM weight refills for latency-sensitive drafting; (2) cross-tree numerical co-design, moving block-scaled Q/K/V preprocessing to HBF and RRAM root plates and enabling block-floating-point (BFP) attention with pipelined softmax reduction in the HBM tree; and (3) HBF-aware SD design-space exploration, revealing how bandwidth-compute provisioning and model scale determine performance, energy, and cost trade-offs. Evaluated across six SD configurations spanning 32B-405B target models, FOREST achieves up to 5.5x end-to-end speedup, 11.46x higher decode throughput, and 16.5x higher decode energy efficiency over NVIDIA A800 GPU-based SD baselines. Under a modeled total cost of ownership, FOREST delivers up to 6.73x higher token-generation cost efficiency.

papers.title: Cruella: A Unified Microscaling and Floating-Point Dot-Product Unit for LLM Inference on FPGAs
papers.abstract: The number formats that accelerators execute natively are fixed at fabrication, yet large language model (LLM) checkpoints are released with MXFP4 weights in the Microscaling (MX) formats standardized in 2023. FPGAs adopt new formats through bitstreams. However, to the best of our knowledge, no deployed FPGA LLM accelerator executes MXFP4 weights alongside BF16 products. We characterize the decoding of MXFP4 checkpoints, whose layers alternate between MXFP4$\times$BF16 products and BF16$\times$BF16 products of attention and BF16 layers. With a BF16 KV cache, BF16$\times$BF16 products take 56%-77% of the datapath time, during which a separate MXFP4 unit idles. We present Cruella, whose unified dot-product unit (UDPU) executes both product types on one DSP array and reduction pipeline. First, per-group pre-alignment keeps this pipeline at the BF16 width and changes perplexity by at most 0.7%. Second, pre-adder packing places two signed MXFP4$\times$BF16 products in one DSP48E2 multiplier with an exact correction. On an Alveo U55C, the UDPU needs 23% fewer DSP slices and 36% fewer LUTs than separate MXFP4 and BF16 units of equal throughput. On this board, MXFP4 weights speed up decoding by 1.15$\times$-1.87$\times$ over BF16 weights, and an NVIDIA A40 GPU decodes faster but spends 0.92$\times$-2.01$\times$ the board's energy per token.

papers.title: BitPrefill: W1.58A4 Tensor-Core Acceleration for Compute-Bound LLM Prefill
papers.abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces large language model (LLM) inference cost, yet implementations optimized for memory-bound decode can leave compute-bound prefill on BF16 tensor cores. This gap matters for input-heavy workloads, including long-context and multimodal applications, where prefill can account for a substantial fraction of inference latency. We propose a W1.58A4 operator that quantizes weights to ternary values and activations to 4-bit, while executing the linear projection on native INT4 general matrix multiply (GEMM) tensor cores, turning prefill from a full-precision matrix multiply into a low-bit one. We deploy the operator for BitNet-b1.58 on a single RTX 4090 and a Jetson Orin Nano edge device, and report GEMM-kernel latency, end-to-end LLMs prefill latency, and task accuracy against bf16 and BitNet/BitBLAS baselines. Our proposed kernel achieves ~1.42x acceleration compared to the original BF16 prefill phase, with negligible reduction on model accuracy.

papers.title: Berth: SLO-Preserving GPU Sharing Without New Preemption
papers.abstract: Inference services keep GPUs reserved for their worst-case load, and most of that capacity sits idle. Filling it with best-effort work such as training is the obvious remedy, and latency is why it rarely happens: on a shared GPU, a request that must finish within milliseconds finds the best-effort job's kernels running or queued ahead of it. Spatial sharing cannot evict them, temporal sharing gives the request only its turn, and hardware partitioning protects it by idling what it does not use. Systems that keep both the SLO and the utilization have reached inside the stack (rewriting kernels, patching the driver, instrumenting the framework), which the operator of a closed GPU stack cannot do. This paper argues that reaching inside is unnecessary. The time-slicer built into commodity GPUs already preempts a running kernel within a fraction of a millisecond and switches the moment a context runs out of work; what it lacks is priority, and priority can be created from outside by controlling what the best-effort context has to run. Berth is a user-space system built on this observation: a preloaded shim feeds the best-effort job to the GPU only when no request needs it (feed control), a declared deadline reference extends the rule to continuous-batching LLM engines, and a shortened best-effort time slice, set without privileges, bounds what a long kernel can cost. Berth changes no application, framework, kernel or driver. Across 31 scenario points with MLPerf SLOs and 13 baselines, Berth meets SLOs within a few percentage points of running alone, above every baseline, with 2.7-3.5x the best-effort throughput of the strongest ones; beside LLM serving, it meets per-token targets for nearly every request while training keeps running. Sharing a closed GPU under SLOs needs no new preemption mechanism, only control over what the existing one sees.

papers.title: VisHead-Spec: Head-Routed Visual Attention for Multimodal Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models(VLMs) while preserving the target model's outputs, but its speedup diminishes under high concurrency serving as the system becomes more compute bounded as the batch size increases. This problem is pronounced for multimodal speculative decoding as the long range of the image tokens in the prompt can significantly increase the computational cost during draft token prediction. The block-diffusion drafters (e.g. DFlash, DSpark) can effectively speed up the draft model efficiency by predicting multiple draft tokens in one forward pass, but their speedup for VLMs under high concurrency is still modest (<9%). In order to understand this gap, we examine the information flow between different modalities from target model to draft model and identify the sparsity pattern of visual attention between the target and draft models: only small set of key-value heads in the draft model need direct visual feature attention in the context and only visual features from top level layers in the target model need to be attended in the context. We therefore propose VisHead-Spec, which selects a small, fixed set of key-value (KV) heads to attend to all image features from top level layers in the target model and restricts the remaining heads to text features. On Qwen3-VL-8B and MMSpec, VisHead-Spec-8 lets 8 of the drafter's 40 KV heads read the image while keeping accepted length within 0.3% of the block-diffusion draft model baseline (i.e. DSpark). At batch size 64, its throughput gain over autoregressive decoding increases to 16.0%, compared with 9.5% for DSpark; at batch size 1, its speedup remains comparable to DSpark.

papers.title: CoPyro: Feeding Copy Proposals to Parallel Drafters
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language generation by letting a target model verify several draft tokens in one forward pass. Earlier neural drafters such as EAGLE extend each candidate sequence one token at a time. Recent work has turned to parallel drafters such as DFlash, which predict a whole block at once. Another approach uses n-gram retrieval to find an earlier occurrence of the current context suffix and copy the tokens that followed it directly into the draft. We introduce CoPyro, which feeds these copied tokens into a parallel drafter in place of masks. The drafter learns from context which tokens to keep and which to revise as it predicts the block in its usual forward pass. Across eight benchmarks on Qwen3-4B, CoPyro improves overall acceptance length for all four parallel drafters tested, with gains of 2.19-5.08% when trained on 100K samples. With DFlash trained on 710K samples, overall gains range from 1.08% to 2.00% across the tested model sizes and temperatures. Code generation benefits most in both settings. On Qwen3-8B, processing the proposals adds an average of 0.24 ms per decoding round in Transformers.

papers.title: HardwareDx: A Foundational Graph Model System for Datacenter Machine Repairs
papers.abstract: The rapid scale-up of AI infrastructure has made datacenter reliability a cornerstone of the cloud business economy. Since hardware failures in hyper-scale AI clusters can stall multi-million dollar training workloads, the downtime of individual machines can cause outsized economic losses. Minimizing machine downtime, therefore, is more important than ever. To address this, we present Hardware Diagnoser (HardwareDx), an AI-driven hardware diagnosis system that applies a graph foundation model approach to automated datacenter maintenance. It allows a single model to diagnose many platforms and accelerate onboarding of new hardware products. Deployed at production scale at Google, HardwareDx yields substantial efficiency gains across diverse compute architectures. Real-world evaluations demonstrate that it reduces production downtime by 18.3% on GPU platforms and 16.1% on TPUs. Furthermore, it significantly accelerates hardware deployment, cutting quality assurance (QA) time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs. These results establish HardwareDx as a field-tested solution for maximizing the reliability and cost efficiency of next generation AI fleets.

papers.title: IndexerStage: Staging Indexer-K across Memory Tiers for Sparse-Attention LLM Serving
papers.abstract: Long-context sparse-attention serving can remain limited by graphics processing unit (GPU) memory after attention data is offloaded. DeepSeek Sparse Attention retains Indexer-K state to select the tokens that attention will read. Its indexer scans this growing state in full at every layer and decode step. A full scan requires the current layer's state, however, not simultaneous residency of every layer. We present IndexerStage, a serving runtime that externalizes Indexer-K state while preserving native GPU score, top-k, and attention kernels. It stages completed pages through shared execution buffers and preserves new entries locally. Joint memory-and-transfer admission checks storage and each layer's transfer demand before accepting a growing batch. The backing tier gathers pages; the model-serving GPU controls transfer timing and byte budgets. We implement IndexerStage in SGLang on 16 model-serving and 16 backing H800 GPUs. Across 16K--64K inputs, local streaming storage occupies 0.65--0.70 GiB per model-serving GPU. Relative to host-memory-backed HiSparse, batch size increases by 12.28--23.08% and decode throughput in tokens per second (TPS) reaches 1.08--1.14x. At 64K with the latent-KV backing path fixed, the larger batch achieves 1.10x decode TPS; enabling streaming at batch size 24 adds 2.42% to time per output token. Mixed-length dynamic serving increases mean generating batch size by 12.07% and delivers 1.31x decode TPS.
